parties:
Sheikh Hasina
Vs.
The State and another
full_judgment:
Md. Shamsul Huda, J: This rule was issued on 18.12.2002 calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the proceeding of Special Case No. 83 of 2002 (formerly Metro. Special Case No. 72 of 2003) bearing BAC G.R. No. 109 of 2001 arising out of Tejgaon P.S. Case No. 36(12) 2001, now pending in the Court of Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka should not be quashed and/ or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 5. In this manner the accused acting in collusion with others and by abuse of power caused loss of the aforesaid sum to the state. After investigation charge sheet being No. 266 dated 11.12.2001 dated 11.12.2001 was submitted in the case against the Petitioner herein along with the then State Minister for Foreign Affairs and others. In the charge sheet it has been observed the necessity of appointment of consultant for advancement of investment in BEPZA, duty free entry of Bangladeshi goods in US market, GSP, protection of labour rights etc. without discussing it with BEPZA, the then Prime Minister, her Principal Secretary, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Foreign Secretary took the decision in a meeting. It was decided to appoint one of the Firms from the list provided by Dr. Samad for which the expenses were to be borne by BEPZA. On recommendation of Dr. Samad, the then Prime Minister approved it on 28.8.2000 and accordingly the Chairman, BEPZA was directed. He then signed an agreement on 12.9.2000 with Dierman Wontley and Zola Inc. which was vetted by the Ministry of Law and approved by the then Prime Minister on 9.11.2000. Since there was no fund available the Finance Ministry was asked for fund allocation. The then Prime Minister directed expeditious payment as it was already delayed and some works had already been done and this proves her involvement in the matter. Initially, the consultant did not submit monthly report, but later they submitted it. Their work was not upto the mark and one para monthly report in one page was submitted which was reviewed by the committee. There was no basis for evaluation of the report by the committee. There was discussion on 27.3.2001 and 31.5.2001 regarding performance of the consultant, instead of monthly evaluation by the committee. In the meeting the committee found the work satisfactory and hence it was decided to receive their service for the remaining period. 

 6. Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner submits that it is admitted in the charge sheet that the petitioner has no role of selection of lobbyist and there is no allegation of any personal gain or mensrea on her part in this regard. In view of the above facts and circumstances as aforesaid that the allegation contained in the F.I.R. and charge sheet do not constitute the offence under Section 418/ 109 of the Penal Code or Section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and the F.I.R. and charge sheet do not disclose any offence committed by her. He submits that the alleged allegations against the accused petitioner are so preposterous even on the admitted facts, no case can stand against the petitioner and as such further prolongation of the prosecution is tantamount to harassment of the petitioner and an abuse of the process of the court. He further submits that the charge sheet against the petitioner has been submitted being politically motivated with intent to politically harass her and to demean, defame, malign and belittle her politically and it was so submitted at the dictation of the persons who were in power on the relevant period and in the circumstances, it is manifestly unjust to allow the process of the criminal proceeding to be continued against the petitioner. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Matin Khasru, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in addition to Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh submits that the instant case was instituted after assuming power by the then ruling party only to politically harass the petitioner inasmuch as it may be mentioned here that the persons in power at the relevant time before October openly proclaimed in series of meetings that if they are elected they would prosecute the petitioner and this case is the result of political grudge. He further submits that from the facts and materials on record it cannot be said that any personal gain or any benefit was taken by the petitioner in appointing the lobbyist. Rather by appointing lobbyist in USA, the then Prime Minister took a bold step to prompt and patronise the garments industry and to increase the export of garments goods in American Market and earned huge foreign exchange for the nation and all the steps which was taken by the petitioner herein are bonafide and at the same time it was done through due process of law and procedure following the rules of business of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. He also submits that no where in the four corners of the F.I.R. and charge sheet any allegation is made that she violated the rules of business by which her power has been allocated as Prime Minister and if Prime Minister cannot exercise her power as per Rules of Business entire government functionaries will be collapsed and with an malafide intention this case has been instituted. He further submits that the then Bureau of Anti Corruption acted illegally due to pressure of the then ruling parties which is not expected from such authority because they are the public servant and they had to proceed as per law to serve the people, who are their real Master, not the ruling party. 

 11. We have asked the learned Advocate for the Anti Corruption Commission to ex-plain by the above averment how a prudent man can presume that the petitioner has played unreasonable roll in directing to pay the dues of the Firm which was appointed as Lobbyist, but he could not explain the same and it was also asked whether this সংশ্লিষ্টতা comes under the purview of any offence. We do not find any reason to believe that by passing the aforesaid order if any, the petitioner has committed any offence, to be punishable under any law of the country and it manifests in the F.I.R. that all the procedure were followed in appointing the Lobbyist and paying their dues / remunerations and it is nowhere in the F.I.R. that by appointing a Lobbyist monitory loss has been caused to the nation. We do not find any reason to initiate such a case against a national leader like the then Prime Minister. 

 16. It is admitted that Bureau of Anti Corruption was guided by the responsible officers of the country and it was functioning as a investigating agency and they are in more higher position than the police, but on reading the F.I.R. and charge sheet of this case, we are unable to accept that an investigating agency like Bureau of Anti Corruption has proceeded bonafide, but it is manifested from very beginning of the case that they have done mischief to the nation by functioning as tools in the hands of the then ruling party. 

 18. In this regard Mr. Abdul Matin Khasru, learned Advocate referred a case of Punjab National Bank and others, appellants Vs. Surendra Prashad Sinha, reported in AIR (1992) (SC) 1815. Wherein it has been held that, "Judicial process should not be an instrument of oppression or needless harassment. The Court should be circumspect and judicious in exercising discretion and should take all the relevant facts and circumstances into consideration before issuing process lest it would be an instrument in the hands of private complainant as vendetta to harass this persons needlessly." 

 19. Before we parting our final decision we want to refer some decisions which has been referred by Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh in support of his contention that the proceeding of a case can be quashed at any initial stage. He referred case of Nasiruddin Mahmud and others Vs. Momtazuddin Ahmed and another, 36 DLR (AD) 14. Wherein it has been held that, "Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the court." 

 20. Cases may also arise where the allegations in the first information report or the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged. In such cases no question of appreciating evidence arises, it is a matter of looking at the complaint or the First Information Report, to decide whether the offence alleged is disclosed or not. In such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the Criminal Court to be issued against the accused person. 

 21. On consideration of series of cases of India and Pakistan jurisdiction our Appellate Division has formulated some criterion in which cases quashing should be appropriate. Reference may be made to 28 DLR (AD)-38 Abdul Quader Chowdhury Vs. The State Wherein it has been held that, " Exercise of its inherent jurisdiction under Section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the High Court depends on the facts of each case- Its interference at the initial stage of a proceeding pending before a court conditioned by the absolute necessity of such interference." 

 22. But a pertinent question may be posed as to when and under what circumstances the said jurisdiction can and should be exercised by the High Court. The consensus of judicial opinion is that it is not possible, desirable or expedient to lay down any inflexible rule which should govern the exercise of this inherent jurisdiction. The exercise of this jurisdiction will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court. 

 23. Categories of cases for quashing of trials before trial court indicated when High Court's inherent jurisdiction under. Section 561 A can be exercised. 

 ii) Some categories of cases may also be inducted where the inherent jurisdiction can and should be exercised for quashing the proceeding. There may be cases where it may be possible for the High Court to take the view that the institution or continuance of criminal proceedings against an accused person may amount to the abuse of the process of the Court or that the quashing of the impugned proceedings would secure the ends of justice. 

 24. If the criminal proceedings in a particular case is in respect of an offence alleged to have been committed by an accused person and it manifestly appears that there is a legal bar against the institution or continuance of the said proceedings the High Court would be justified in quashing the proceedings on that ground. 

 25. Cases may also arise where the allegations in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged, in such case no question of appreciating evidence arises; it is a matter merely of looking at the complaint or the First Information Report to decide whether the offence alleged is disclosed or not. In such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the criminal court to be issued against the accused person. 

 26. Third categories of the cases: 

 28. The settled principle of law is that to bring a case within the purview of section 561A for the purpose of quashing a proceeding one of the following conditions must be fulfilled: 

 (6) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused; 

 (9) In a case where the allegations in the F.I.R. or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged and 

 29. In this regard we may refer to a decision of the case of Begum Khaleda Zia Vs. State, reported in 55 DLR, 596. Wherein it has been held that, "Criminal intention is sine qua non for an offence under section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. When a decision is taken collectively or even individually by following the rules of procedure or the rules of business criminal intention be-hind such decision should not normally be inferred." 

 30. The above principle of the case of Begum Khaleda Zia is fully applicable in the present case and it can be a guide line for taking decision in such type of cases, wherein the petitioner herein is an accused. 

 31. We are in respectful agreement with Mr. Justice Md. Joynul Abedin, (as his Lord-ship then was) the author Judge of the judgment as referred above, that without any criminal intention a head of the Government cannot be prosecuted so lightly to damage or destroy her political image and if this culture is allowed to be continued the investigating agencies as well as the court also will not be able to exercise its prudence freely and impartially and this culture is detrimental to the nation as a whole, because in a democratic country it is usual that power will be changed from persons to persons and after assuming the power if the public servants are used in the manner which is evident from the present case, this will be serious threat to the nation and the general people as well. So it is at least expected that starting of criminal cases for harassment of the Government Functionaries, Specially the Head of the Government and the public servants will be stopped hence forth, because those will at least destroy the valuable time of the Court, to deal with those cases. 

 33. Mr. Sayed Mizanur Rahaman, Advocate for the A.C.0 raised objection as to maintainability of the quashing petition on the ground that before framing of charge or without filing any application for discharge under section 241A of the Code of criminal procedure the instant application under section-561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is premature. We have given our anxious thought over this point. Section 241A and section 561 A are two independent sections of the Code. Section 241 A speaks of discharge of an accused before trial where charge is found to be groundless and 561A is the inherent power of the High Court Division and this power can be exercised in case of abuse of process of court and for securing the ends of Justice. 

 36. Section 265C in Chapter 23 speaks of discharge of an accused in a trial before Court of Sessions; section 241A in Chapter 20 speaks of discharge of an accused in a trial by a Magistrate. These are two independent sections of the Code which deal with discharge of an accused brought for trial in respect of cases triable by a Court of Sessions and by a Court of Magistrate. These two sections indicate that when an accused is brought for trial before a court of law the court upon hearing the parties and on consideration of the record of the case and the documents may discharge the accused. These two sections having nothing to do with quashing of a proceeding. Section 561A is an independent inherent power of the High Court Division and this power can be exercised in case of abuse of process of court and for securing the ends of justice and or to give effect to any order under the Code. Practice and procedure 

 37. It is very surprising that the High Court Division enunciated a wrong proposition of law without entering into the merit of the case. This is not only illegal but also not a proper exercise of jurisdiction vested in the court itself. 

 38. The High Court Division can quash the proceeding of a Criminal Case under Section 561A Cr. P. C. even during police investigation if no cognizable offence is disclosed. This view has been approved in the Case of Emperior Vs. Nazir Ahmed, A. I. R. (32)1945 P.C. 18 and the view that it will be Premature to invok 561A Cr. P. C. before availing of the remedy Provided in 241-A Cr. P. C. and 265C Cr. P. C. has been disapproved by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Appellate Division as being not Correct. 

 39. On this point further reference may be made to the case of Sayed Mohammad Hashem alias Hashim Vs. The State: reported in 1995 BLT (AD) 129. 

 41. On consideration of the above decisions and also some other decisions such as the case of the State of Haryana and others Vs. Bhajan Lal and others, reported in AIR (1992) (SC) 604, we hold that the F.I.R. as well as the charge sheet of the instant case do not disclose any offence against the petitioner herein and even on the admitted facts no case can stand against her and further prolongation of the proceeding would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court and it is so preposterous that if the allegations made in the FIR and charge sheet are taken in their entirety no criminal case is made out against the petitioner, rather this is an outcome of political vengeance and as such we hold that prolongation of the proceeding will be an abuse of the process of the court and this still born child has fouled the judicial process so much so that the sooner it is buried, the better. 

 42. In the result, the rule is made absolute and the proceeding of Special Case No. 83 of 2002 (formerly Metro: Special Case NO. 72 of 2003) bearing BAC G.R. No. 109 of 2001 arising out of Tejgaon P.S. Case No. 36(12) 2001, now pending in the Court of Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka is quashed in respect of the petitioner.
